## Assignment description

In 2013, *n* = 1453 old people underwent surgery for leg fractures.
We recorded baseline information, and contacted them one year later,
asking them:

- y1 = to what degree they can move their broken leg (0-100)
- y2 = if they still have pain (0/1)

Available information: hosp, severity, sex, age, bmi, edu, smoking habits, alcohol consumption, milk consumption, comorbidities, partner, city.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
lab4_dat <- readRDS("data4.Rds")
str(lab4_dat) # Should show data.frame with 1453 obs of 17 variables
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

### Question 2

Fit a linear regression model with y1 as response and smoke as predictor. What is the sample mean of y1 among smokers and non-smokers? Is the difference statistically significant?

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" collapse="true" title="Answer"}

The sample mean among non-smokers is 68 and among smokers 54. The difference is statistically significant because the p-value for the test of whether the coefficient for smoke is zero is small.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
summary(lm(y1 ~ smoke, lab4_dat))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

Call:

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)  68.1286     0.3668  185.71   <2e-16 ***
smoke       -14.2874     1.0725  -13.32   <2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 13.14 on 1451 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.109,	Adjusted R-squared:  0.1084
```

### Question 3

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" collapse="true" title="Answer"}

### Question 4

Fit the same model as in Question 3 but add a term I(bmi^2) and test whether its coefficient is equal to zero. What does I(bmi^2) tell us?

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" collapse="true" title="Answer"}

Bmi has a linear association of 3.7. But in addition, we now have a quadratic association I(bmi^2), which modifies the linear association as a person gets higher bmi. As a person gets higher bmi, the positive effect of bmi on y1 decreases, and eventually reverses. The p-value for both bmi terms is significant.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
summary(lm(y1 ~ smoke + age + sex + bmi + I(bmi^2) + city + partner + edu + alcohol, lab4_dat))
```

### Question 5

Interpret the intercept in the model in Question 4.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" collapse="true" title="Answer"}

The intercept is the estimated average y1 for a person who does not smoke, is female, is aged 0, has bmi 0, lives in a large city, and so on, so that all predictors are zero. Such a person does not exist, so even though we can technically say that is what the intercept is, it has no practical meaning in this setting.
:::

### Question 6

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" collapse="true" title="Answer"}

### Question 7

Is there evidence age is an important predictor? Test whether the coefficients for age, age^2, and age^3 are all zero.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" collapse="true" title="Answer"}

No, in that output neither of the age coefficients are significantly different from zero individually.

The F-test shows the age variable is important: we reject the null hypothesis that the smaller model, which does not include age, is equivalent to the larger model. Same conclusion with AIC and BIC. The conclusion is that we should have age in our model, but not with a linear, quadratic and cubic term. A simpler (e.g. linear) effect of age will suffice.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
fit_q7 <- lm(y1 ~ smoke + age + I(age^2) + I(age^3) + sex + bmi + city + partner + edu + alcohol, lab4_dat)
summary(fit_q7)
```

### Question 8

Fit a logistic regression model for y2 where the regressors are the same as in Question 3. Interpret the output.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" collapse="true" title="Answer"}

The output indicates that smoking does not affect the probability of still having pain, but some of the other covariates do. For example, males are more likely to experience pain on average, holding everything else fixed, while having a partner decreases the probability of pain.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
summary(glm(y2 ~ smoke + age + sex + bmi + city + partner + edu + alcohol,
            data = lab4_dat, family = binomial))
```

### Question 9

Use a likelihood ratio test to test whether education is an important predictor in the model in Question 8.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" collapse="true" title="Answer"}

We do not reject the null hypothesis that the coefficient for education is zero, so education does not seem to be an important predictor in this model.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
anova(glm(y2 ~ smoke + age + sex + bmi + city + partner + edu + alcohol,
            data = lab4_dat, family = binomial),
      glm(y2 ~ smoke + age + sex + bmi + city + partner + alcohol,
          data = lab4_dat, family = binomial),
      test = "LRT")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
